forecasts.label: Interest payable

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Tower Hamlets forecasts £30.0m schools-grant overspend, with government to write off up to £32m of earlier deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Tower Hamlets forecasts a £30.0m overspend this year on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, almost all of it in high needs, the part that funds special educational needs. The Quarter 2 budget monitoring report to Cabinet on 12 November says this would take the grant's deficit to £65.2m at the end of 2026/27, from £35.2m at the start. The paper estimates £89m by 31 March 2028.

The Department for Education has approved the council's special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) reform plan. That makes the council eligible for a high needs stability grant, which the paper says will write off up to 90% (£32m) of the £35.2m brought-forward high needs deficit. The council expects the grant in late November or early December. The Department has not yet clarified the remaining 10%, £3.5m as at 31 March 2026. The deficit is held in an unusable reserve under the statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps it off the main balance sheet and ends on 1 April 2028. If the council must fund 10% of the 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits, £8.9m would go into the 2028/29 budget as a one-off cost.

Education is forecast at a £4.6m net overspend for 2026/27, £2.2m higher than the £2.4m forecast at the previous period. The paper cites SEND costs including transport, with increased demand. Separately, the council reports a capital programme of about £4.8m for SEND and accessibility work in mainstream schools, and £6.3m secured for alternative provision places.

news_drafts.headline: Tower Hamlets schools grant deficit reached £35.2m; government 90% grant due Autumn 2026
news_drafts.lead:
Tower Hamlets ended 2025/26 with a cumulative deficit of £35.2m on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, at 31 March 2026. The in-year overspend was £15.1m. Papers for the Audit Committee on 4 November say a 90% government grant on the deficit "will be paid in Autumn 2026, subject to each local authority submitting" a local reform plan for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) and securing approval from the Department for Education.

The grant covers the deficit in high needs, the part of school funding for children with SEND, accrued up to the end of 2025/26. The deficit sits within the ring-fenced schools budget. The papers also say government does not expect councils to fund future SEND costs from general funds from 1 April 2028.

The council's corporate risk register, dated 19 October 2026, records a £19.2m overspend forecast at period 2 of 2026/27. It names adult social care, SEND and homelessness as areas affected nationally. The register lists spending control panels for adult social care, SEND and temporary accommodation, plus weekly Spending Review Panels chaired by the Mayor. It gives the financial risk a current score of 20.

news_drafts.headline: Tower Hamlets' auditors now expect a clean accounts opinion by 2028/29 at the earliest, not 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Tower Hamlets Council's external auditor, EY, now expects the earliest date for a fully unqualified opinion on the council's accounts to be 2028/29, two years later than the 2026/27 the council had aimed for. An addendum to EY's 2025/26 audit plan, put to the Audit Committee on 24 September 2026, says the earlier target is "premature". It says updated audit guidance (LARRIG 06) is "in part outdated".

The 2025/26 audit will examine only the closing balances on the balance sheet. The full audit of income and spending, and of the balance sheet, is deferred to 2026/27. EY expects to gain assurance over unusable reserves, such as the pension reserve, by the end of 2025/26. For usable reserves, the part the council can actually spend, it says "it will take a few years".

A briefing paper to the committee says the council's progress is "behind the expected timescales" set out in the national recovery guidance (LARRIG 01), because "limited procedures were completed for 2023/24 and 2024/25". That prevented a move on from a disclaimer opinion, where auditors give no opinion at all. The briefing links this to a significant weakness and a statutory recommendation on the council's arrangements for financial reporting. It notes that 87% of local government bodies met the earlier deadlines for producing statements, but that "quality and completeness – not speed" held back audit progress.

The pension fund papers show a related problem. EY issued a disclaimer on the £1,620m present value of promised retirement benefits in 2024/25. Its reports have recorded errors in the membership data given to the actuary every year since 31 March 2019. The fund has engaged external consultants to correct the data, and EY is testing the results. The outcome is not yet confirmed.

For 2025/26 the base audit fee is £91,183, still to be confirmed. EY lists modified opinions among the factors that could add work. The fund's net assets were £2,192m at 31 March 2025, including £355m of unquoted investments valued on management judgement. Both the Corporate Director, Resources, and the Head of Pensions and Treasury are interim appointments.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026-27 Quarter 2 General Fund Variance Movement
findings.headline: Integrated Commissioning reported a structural budget gap of £1.3m for client transport and £1.2m for Care Technology Transformation at P2
findings.detail: The P2 variance of £2.5m was attributed to these structural budget gaps. At Q2 the forecast net overspend is £4.8m, with an additional £2.3m of variance reported.
findings.matters: A structural gap, as opposed to a one-off overspend, means the base budget needs to change, which is a governance point for other councils facing similar transport and care technology costs.
findings.figures: £1.3m client transport structural gap; £1.2m Care Technology Transformation; £2.5m P2 variance; £4.8m Q2 forecast net overspend; £2.3m adverse movement
findings.quote: Structural budget gap: client transport - £1.3m and Care Technology Transformation

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026-27 Quarter 2 General Fund Variance Movement
findings.headline: £0.5m of Tackling Poverty costs held pending agreement to use of reserves
findings.detail: The paper says the Tackling Poverty costs of £0.5m are pending agreement to use reserves, so the spend is not yet funded.
findings.matters: Spending that depends on a reserve decision not yet taken is a point a finance director would track against the reserve balance.
findings.figures: £0.5m Tackling Poverty costs pending agreement to use of reserves
findings.quote: Net overspend due to the costs for Tackling Poverty of £0.5m pending agreement to use of reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026-27 Quarter 2 General Fund Variance Movement
findings.headline: Education forecast £4.6m net overspend, £2.2m higher than P2, with SEND costs cited
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to SEND costs including transport, education psychology and EHCP admin staff, driven by increased demand. It also notes traded income shortfalls in parental engagement and Gorsefield.
findings.matters: SEND demand and transport costs are a widely shared pressure, and a council-by-council breakdown of the drivers is useful to peers.
findings.figures: £4.6m Q2 forecast net overspend; £2.4m P2 forecast net overspend; £2.2m adverse movement
findings.quote: Increased costs related to SEND (incl Transport)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026-27 Quarter 2 General Fund Variance Movement
findings.headline: Corporate budgets record a £6.0m favourable movement from releasing unallocated inflation provision and a £5m reduction in MRP
findings.detail: The paper attributes £1m to release of the unallocated inflation provision and £5m to a reduction in minimum revenue provision for debt financing.
findings.matters: A reduction in MRP changes the council's annual charge for debt repayment, which lenders and finance directors track when assessing debt management.
findings.figures: £(6.0)m combined favourable movement; £1m unallocated inflation provision release; £5m MRP reduction
findings.quote: Release of unallocated inflation provision (£1m) and deduction in Minium Revenue Provision (debt financing) of £5m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2026-27 Quarter 2 General Fund Variance Movement
findings.headline: Culture forecast £2.4m net overspend, driven by a £2.1m leisure income shortfall
findings.detail: The paper says the leisure income shortfall is partly offset by in-year mitigations across Culture of £0.5m and CIL substitutions of £1.2m.
findings.matters: Leisure income shortfalls are a recurring pressure for councils running their own leisure services, and the mitigation mix shows how one council is covering it.
findings.figures: £2.1m leisure income shortfall; £0.5m Culture mitigations; £1.2m CIL substitutions; £2.4m Q2 net overspend; £0.4m movement from P2
findings.quote: additional income shortfall in leisure (£2.1m) offset by in year mitigations across Culture (£0.5m) and CIL substitutions
